text.hook:
"deque `push_back` keeps my iterators valid."
References survive. Iterators do not.

The full invalidation table, plus 6 myths. Swipe ➜ and save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. Three ways an iterator breaks
2. vector rules, with and without reallocation
3. deque, list, map, unordered, array
4. Safe erase patterns
5. What debug tools catch and miss
6. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: What survives each container operation, and why "it still prints the right value" proves nothing.

slides.title: Three ways an iterator breaks

cards.label: Storage moved
cards.text: Elements copied or moved to a new buffer: vector or string reallocation.

cards.label: Position shifted
cards.text: Same slot, different element: vector insert or erase **without** reallocation.

cards.label: Bookkeeping changed
cards.text: Element stays put, the iterator's internals do not: deque map, unordered buckets.

slides.takeaway: On an invalid iterator you may only assign or destroy it. Even `it == v.end()` is UB.

slides.title: What dies after each call
slides.takeaway: `insert` and `erase` return the iterator to continue from. Always use it.

slides.title: Insert vs erase, per layout
rows: end insert: all iterators, **no** refs. End erase: only the erased one (+ `end()` at the back)
insert: nothing. Erase: only the erased element
rehash: all iterators, **no** refs or pointers
never invalidated while the array lives
slides.takeaway: Node containers never move elements: pointers and references survive everything but erasing that element.

slides.title: Erasing while iterating
items: `map`/`set` loop: `it = m.erase(it);` returns the next node (C++11)
Never change the size inside a range-for: its `end()` is cached

slides.title: What catches a stale iterator
rows: singular iterators, wrong container. Misses: old `end()` after `push_back` (GCC 11)
use after reallocation, out of bounds. Misses: shifted elements
`operator[]` out of range. Does not track iterators
slides.takeaway: Debug mode changes the ABI and is slow: run it in tests and CI.

slides.hero:
Validity is defined
by the operation,
not by the address.
slides.lead: An invalid iterator can still point at allocated, readable memory. "It printed a sensible value" proves nothing.

items.truth: It relinks nodes. Every iterator stays valid and follows its element.

items.myth: "Comparing an invalid iterator with `end()` is harmless."
items.truth: Any use other than assignment or destruction is UB.
Erasing at either end invalidates only the erased element (plus `end()` for `pop_back`).
References and pointers survive. Iterators do not.
They stay valid, but now point into the other container (`end()` may not).
It only sees freed or out-of-bounds memory. Shifted elements look valid to it.

slides.hero:
Check the rule
for that container
and that call.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
This loop already uses it = v.erase(it).
The reviewer said: "Correct now, ship it."

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: No crash, no sanitizer report. Read the loop header twice.

slides.title:
Remove every 2.
What does it print?

bullets: `it = v.erase(it)` already points at the **next** element: the second 2.
The loop header's `++it` then skips it. Double advance.
No UB with this input: `it` is always valid. It is a logic bug.
With `{1, 3, 2}` it becomes UB: erasing the last element returns `end()`, then `++it` steps past it.
slides.wrong: "B: erase invalidates it" (it was reassigned first)

slides.title: Advance only when nothing was erased
slides.tip: Both print `1 3`. The loop is O(n²) on a vector; `erase_if` is O(n).
slides.takeaway: When the header increments, the body must not move the iterator too.

text.hook:
Capacity is reserved. Nothing reallocates.
So the iterator to 300 is still fine. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The buffer address does not change. ASan stays silent.

slides.title:
No reallocation.
What does `*it` give?

slides.verdict_sub: Observed with GCC 11, libstdc++: prints 200. ASan: silent
bullets: Without reallocation, `insert` invalidates every iterator **at or after** the insertion point.
The buffer did not move, so `it` still addresses slot 2, which now holds the old `v[1]`: wrong data, no crash.
`-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG` aborts: "attempt to dereference a singular iterator".
slides.wrong: "300: capacity was reserved, so nothing is invalidated"

slides.title: Re-derive positions after the insert
slides.tip: Or keep an index and bump it when the insert lands at or before it. `insert` returns an iterator to the new element.
slides.takeaway: Validity is defined by the operation, not by whether memory moved.

text.hook:
Print every second element.
it += 2, stop at end(). Three lines, looks fine.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Tests with an even size pass every time.

slides.title:
Every second element.
What happens?

slides.verdict_sub: Our GCC 11 run: 10 30 50, then garbage, then a segfault
bullets: So `it != v.end()` is never false. Forming that iterator is already UB.
ASan: `heap-buffer-overflow`. `-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG`: "attempt to advance ... outside its valid range".
With an even size the loop lands exactly on `end()`, so the bug hides.

slides.title: Check the distance before stepping
slides.tip: `std::next(it, 2)` does not check bounds either. `it < v.end()` still forms the bad iterator.
slides.takeaway: `!=` only works when every step can land exactly on `end()`.

text.hook:
Find the 3 from the back with a reverse iterator.
Then erase it with rit.base(). Clean, short, compiles.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: One of those bugs that only shows up in the output.

slides.title:
Intended to erase the 3.
What does it print?

bullets: A reverse iterator stores `base()`, which points **one past** the element it refers to.
If the found value were the last element, `rit.base()` would be `end()`, and `erase(end())` is UB.
slides.wrong: "1 2 4 5: base() converts rit to the same element"

slides.title: Step once, then take base()
slides.tip: `*rit` is always `*std::prev(rit.base())`. That is why `rbegin().base() == end()`.
slides.takeaway: Erase through a reverse iterator with `std::next(rit).base()`.
